North Dakota State enters the 2026 NCAA Tournament at 27-7 overall after finishing 14-2 in Summit League play and then winning the Summit League tournament title game 70-62 over North Dakota on March 8, 2026. ESPN’s team page listed the Bison at 24-7 after the regular season, and the tournament wins over Oral Roberts, Omaha, and North Dakota pushed the final pre-NCAA mark to 27-7. Their regular-season title was clinched at 14-2, and the March 8 championship box score listed them at 27-7 and 14-2 in league play. In short: exact record, 27-7 overall, 14-2 Summit. ([espn.com](https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/team/stats/_/id/2449/sort/fieldGoalsMade))

From a traditional scouting standpoint, NDSU’s offense is built on experienced guard decision-making, paint touches that collapse the defense, and kick-out threes from role players who know exactly where the ball is supposed to go. The clearest statistical markers are Andy Stefonowicz at 4.8 assists per game, Damari Wheeler-Thomas at 14.1 points per game, Trevian Carson at 12.2 points and 6.5 rebounds, and Tay Smith shooting 39.5 percent from three. The game recaps repeatedly show the structure: late-clock creation by Stefonowicz, downhill scoring by Wheeler-Thomas, interior finishing or short-roll play from Noah Feddersen, and weak-side spot-up shooting from Tay Smith or Carson. In the Jan. 22 win at Denver, the sequence that closed the game was textbook NDSU half-court offense: with the game tied 72-72, Feddersen scored “a bucket in traffic,” then Stefonowicz buried a contested corner three with 26 seconds left. In the March 5 tournament win over Oral Roberts, when ORU cut it to 57-52, Wheeler-Thomas answered with a three and the Bison then scored eight straight, again showing a guard-led response rather than random isolation basketball. ([espn.com](https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/team/stats/_/id/2449/sort/fieldGoalsMade))

Specific offensive tendencies show up in the shot profile and scoring distribution. Against North Dakota on Feb. 28, NDSU hit 16-of-29 from three in a 96-63 win, with Tay Smith scoring a career-high 28 points on seven made threes and Stefonowicz adding 15 points with six assists. That game reflected their best version: drive-and-kick spacing, extra-pass threes, and guards controlling tempo once the defense starts rotating. Against Kansas City on Jan. 8, NDSU led wire-to-wire in a 97-73 road win, another sign that when they establish rhythm early, Richman’s group will run structured secondary break into half-court action instead of playing loose. The fact that Stefonowicz led the team in assists and shot 40.2 percent from three indicates he is not just a pure point guard; he is the organizer in ball-screen and inside-out action who must be chased over screens. ([gobison.com](https://gobison.com/news/2026/3/1/mens-basketball-bison-pound-und-to-set-regular-season-win-record-96-63.aspx?utm_source=openai))

Defensively, the Bison profile as a fundamentally sound man-to-man team that prioritizes keeping games in front, finishing possessions on the glass, and shrinking the lane without giving away total control of the arc. Their best defensive performances were low-possession and physical. They beat Jacksonville State 56-43 on Nov. 26 by “locking down defensively,” held Omaha to 50 points in the Summit semifinal on March 7, and limited Oral Roberts to 38 percent shooting on March 5. They also won the Summit title game while holding North Dakota to 62 points. The rebounding numbers matter here: Feddersen had 13 rebounds versus Omaha in the semifinal and 11 rebounds versus Oral Roberts in the quarterfinal, showing how NDSU finishes stops. Trevian Carson, a guard, leads the team at 6.5 rebounds per game and 1.9 steals, which tells you Richman values gang rebounding and active nail/help defense from the perimeter. ([gobison.com](https://gobison.com/news/2025/11/26/mens-basketball-ndsu-shuts-down-jax-state-for-56-43-victory.aspx?utm_source=openai))

The defensive weakness is that they can be vulnerable when opponents get hot early from three and force them to play uphill. The Feb. 26 loss at St. Thomas is the best example. St. Thomas made five threes in the first five minutes, jumped out 28-13, and led 50-27 at halftime. NDSU lost 84-62 while allowing 56 percent shooting. Likewise, in the Feb. 5 home loss to Denver, the Bison surrendered 51 percent shooting and lost 78-71 after Denver repeatedly answered once the game got tight. Those two games reveal the stress point: if the opponent’s shot-making pulls NDSU’s help defenders outward and prevents them from controlling the paint and glass, the Bison become more ordinary. ([gobison.com](https://gobison.com/news/2026/2/27/mens-basketball-st-thomas-knocks-off-bison.aspx))

David Richman’s coaching philosophy is visible in the way this team wins close games and responds after counters. He was named Summit League Coach of the Year in 2025-26, his second such honor after 2014-15. His teams are typically disciplined, senior-driven, and situationally sharp. There are documented examples of in-game adjustment. On Jan. 17 against St. Thomas, after the Tommies scored five straight to cut it to 66-63 late, Wheeler-Thomas attacked the rim for a layup through contact with 27 seconds left to seal a 68-65 win; that is a clear late-game shift from purely clock-draining offense to direct rim pressure. On March 5 versus Oral Roberts, when ORU made a 10-0 run to trim the margin to five, NDSU answered immediately with a Wheeler-Thomas three and an eight-point response, a sign of Richman calling something to halt momentum rather than letting the game drift. On Feb. 28 against North Dakota, after falling behind 17-8, NDSU closed on an 88-46 run, which speaks to an effective tactical and emotional reset during the first half. ([gobison.com](https://gobison.com/news/2026/3/3/mens-basketball-four-bison-men-claim-summit-league-honors-richman-named-coach-of-the-year.aspx?utm_source=openai))

Clutch and late-game execution is one of NDSU’s strongest tournament-selling points. The best example is Jan. 10 at Omaha: Wheeler-Thomas scored a layup as time expired for a 78-76 comeback win. On Jan. 22 at Denver, tied 72-72 in the final two minutes, Feddersen scored inside, added two free throws on the next trip, and Stefonowicz drilled the dagger corner three with 0:26 left in an 82-77 win. On Jan. 17 against St. Thomas, Wheeler-Thomas scored a driving layup through contact with 27 seconds left to close a 68-65 win over the preseason league favorite. Even the Feb. 18 win at South Dakota State showed composure: SDSU cut it to 52-51 with 9:00 left, but NDSU never surrendered the lead and won 74-66. ([gobison.com](https://gobison.com/news/2026/1/10/mens-basketball-wheeler-thomas-buzzer-beater-caps-bison-comeback-at-omaha.aspx?utm_source=openai))

The key players start with Wheeler-Thomas, the lead scorer at 14.1 points per game. He is the primary late-clock attacker and the best clutch shot creator on the roster. His signature moments were the buzzer-beating layup at Omaha on Jan. 10 and 19 points in the Summit title game on March 8. Trevian Carson averages 12.2 points and 6.5 rebounds and gives them wing toughness; he scored 23 points at Denver on Jan. 22 and grabbed 10 rebounds in the title game. Stefonowicz averages 9.4 points and a team-best 4.8 assists while shooting 40.2 percent from three; he is the connective passer and late-clock decision-maker, with eight assists in the March 7 semifinal and the late dagger three at Denver. Feddersen averages 9.3 points, 4.7 rebounds, and a team-best 1.1 blocks; he posted back-to-back double-doubles in Sioux Falls, 12 points and 11 rebounds versus Oral Roberts, then 11 points and 13 rebounds versus Omaha. Treyson Anderson adds 10.5 points and 5.5 rebounds and had 16 points in the semifinal. Tay Smith is the specialist shooter; his career-high 28 points and seven threes against North Dakota on Feb. 28 showed exactly how dangerous NDSU becomes when a floor-spacer catches rhythm. ([espn.com](https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/team/stats/_/id/2449/sort/fieldGoalsMade))

Their notable wins tell the story of a mature mid-major champion. The Jan. 17 win over St. Thomas, 68-65, snapped the Tommies’ nine-game winning streak and showed NDSU could win a grinder against the preseason favorite. The Jan. 22 road win at Denver, 82-77, showed poise in a tie game inside the final two minutes. The Feb. 18 win at South Dakota State, 74-66, was their 10th road win, matching a school record, and reinforced that they can control tempo away from Fargo. The Feb. 28 demolition of North Dakota, 96-63, showed their offensive ceiling. Then the Summit tournament run showed defensive championship form: 76-65 over Oral Roberts, 74-50 over Omaha, and 70-62 over North Dakota. ([gobison.com](https://gobison.com/news/2026/1/17/mens-basketball-bison-defeat-st-thomas-in-battle-of-summit-league-unbeatens-68-65.aspx?utm_source=openai))

The notable losses are just as revealing. The 78-71 home loss to Denver on Feb. 5 exposed problems when opponents shoot efficiently and force NDSU to chase from behind; Denver shot 51 percent while NDSU shot 40 percent and only 6-of-20 from three. The 84-62 loss at St. Thomas on Feb. 26 exposed their vulnerability to early three-point avalanches and first-half pressure; the Tommies made five threes in the first five minutes and led 50-27 at the half. The 79-77 loss at North Dakota on Feb. 22 also matters because Eli King blocked a final Bison shot in the paint, a reminder that even this veteran group can get stalled into contested late possessions. ([gobison.com](https://gobison.com/news/2026/2/5/mens-basketball-denver-snaps-ndsu-win-streak.aspx?utm_source=openai))

Richman’s NCAA tournament history is straightforward and relevant. NDSU’s official staff biography says that in 2018-19 he coached the Bison to the NCAA Tournament and a First Four win over North Carolina Central, giving him one NCAA tournament victory as head coach. That 2019 team then lost in the Round of 64 to Duke. In 2014-15, Richman’s first team also reached the NCAA Tournament and lost in the Round of 64. So entering 2026, Richman’s head-coaching NCAA tournament history is: 2015 Round of 64, 2019 First Four win then Round of 64 loss, and now 2026 as the current qualifier. ([gobison.com](https://gobison.com/staff-directory/david-richman-02-05-/178?utm_source=openai))

Bottom line: North Dakota State is a veteran, execution-heavy, guard-led team that wins with structure. The Bison are at their best when Wheeler-Thomas gets downhill, Stefonowicz controls the game, Feddersen cleans the glass, Carson supplies two-way wing production, and their shooters punish help. Their best evidence is not theoretical; it is on the tape and in the results: 27-7 overall, 14-2 in the Summit, multiple late-game wins, and a conference tournament run that held Omaha to 50 and North Dakota to 62. ([espn.com](https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/boxscore/_/gameId/401851629?utm_source=openai))

North Dakota State enters the 2026 NCAA Tournament as a profile that is stronger on possession-by-possession quality than on résumé heft. The Bison won the Summit League regular season at 14-2, are 24-7 against Division I competition, and drew Michigan State for Thursday, March 19, 2026. Their résumé metrics are dragged down by schedule quality more than by raw performance: WarrenNolan lists NDSU at NET No. 114, with ESPN BPI No. 133, KenPom No. 113, and Bart Torvik T-Rank No. 114. The same team sheet shows a NET strength of schedule of 350 and non-conference SOS of 336, which is the central fact shaping how the committee and predictive systems see them. They simply did not have many chances to accrue high-end wins, and in fact they finished 0-0 in Quadrant 1, 0-1 in Quadrant 2, 5-4 in Quadrant 3, and 19-2 in Quadrant 4. ([warrennolan.com](https://www.warrennolan.com/basketball/2026/team-net-sheet?team=North-Dakota-State))

The underlying efficiency picture is more favorable than the résumé. WarrenNolan’s 2026 advanced-stat pages list North Dakota State with an offensive rating of 114.2 points per 100 possessions, good for No. 74 nationally, and a defensive rating of 102.7, good for No. 56. That implies a +11.5 net efficiency margin, which is the profile of a solid, well-balanced mid-major rather than a typical bottom-seeded auto-bid. Pace is measured at 68.1 possessions per 40 minutes, ranking 192nd nationally, so this is basically a middle-tempo team: not a pure grinder, not an all-out transition group, but comfortable playing in a normal-possession game. ([warrennolan.com](https://www.warrennolan.com/basketball/2026/stats-adv-offensive-rating))

Their shot-quality and shot-selection indicators are fairly clean. WarrenNolan gives the Bison an effective field goal percentage of 53.4%, No. 87 nationally. The same source lists a 3-point attempt rate of 0.427, No. 123 nationally, and a free-throw attempt rate of 0.307, No. 291 nationally. In plain terms: NDSU takes a healthy amount of threes, hits enough of them to matter, but does not live at the foul line. That matches the official team totals from NDSU: 979-of-2091 from the field (.468), 320-of-876 from three (.365), and 467-of-644 at the line (.725), while averaging 80.7 points per game. Converting those season totals yields an eFG% of 54.5%, almost identical to WarrenNolan’s 53.4% D-I-only figure and a nice cross-check on the team’s offensive identity. ([warrennolan.com](https://www.warrennolan.com/basketball/2026/stats-adv-efg-percent))

On the Four Factors-style breakdown, the best directly available numbers are strongest for shooting and offensive rebounding. WarrenNolan lists North Dakota State’s offensive rebound rate at 33.6%, No. 77 nationally, and NDSU’s own cumulative stats show key frontcourt rebound production from Trevian Carson (219 rebounds, 73 offensive), Treyson Anderson (183, 57 offensive), and Noah Feddersen (174, 56 offensive). Using those official individual totals, the team offensive-rebound share comes out to 31.9% overall, while the D-I-only WarrenNolan number is 33.6%; the difference is consistent with differing game pools, but both point to the same conclusion: NDSU is a legitimately good second-chance offense. Turnover rate is not directly posted in the sources I found, but using the official totals produces an approximate offensive TO% of 16.4%, which suggests they are reasonably secure with the ball rather than elite or sloppy. ([warrennolan.com](https://www.warrennolan.com/basketball/2026/stats-adv-orb-percent))

Defensively, the Bison are better than casual observers might assume from the mid-major label. Their 102.7 defensive rating ranks 56th nationally, and opponent shooting in the official cumulative stats is modest: foes have shot .438 overall and .335 from three. From those same totals, opponent eFG% works out to about 51.1%, which is solid containment. NDSU also appears to finish possessions fairly well on the defensive glass; using opponent rebound totals from the official stats, opponents grabbed roughly 20.9% of their missed shots on offense. What the Bison do not do, at least in the same official totals, is generate a huge number of turnovers; an approximate forced TO% from the raw season stats comes out around 9.2%, implying their defense is more about making teams score over structure than about chaos and live-ball disruption. ([warrennolan.com](https://www.warrennolan.com/basketball/2026/stats-adv-defensive-rating))

Recent form is strong, though not spotless. NDSU finished the regular season 24-7 overall and 14-2 in the Summit, then won the conference tournament by beating Omaha 74-50 and North Dakota 70-62. Over the last 10 games visible on ESPN’s schedule, they went 8-2: losses to Denver on February 5 and at St. Thomas on February 26, but wins over Omaha twice, North Dakota twice, South Dakota State on the road, Kansas City, and the two Summit tournament games. That late stretch suggests a team playing above its raw national résumé ranking, especially because it included a road win at South Dakota State and dominant wins over Omaha and Kansas City. The most recent data point before the NCAA Tournament is positive: they closed with three straight wins, capped by the Summit title. ([espn.com](https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/team/schedule/_/id/2449/season/2026))

The biggest divergence between the numbers and conventional wisdom is that North Dakota State does not look like a classic overmatched 14/15-seed profile. The public shorthand for a Summit auto-bid is usually “good little offense, weak defense, flimsy résumé.” But NDSU’s profile is actually balanced: top-75 offense, top-60 defense, top-90 eFG%, top-80 offensive rebounding, and a perfectly respectable middle-of-the-pack pace. The reason they are seeded like a dangerous underdog rather than evaluated like an at-large team is the schedule. A NET of 114 with an SOS of 350 tells the story: the efficiency base is credible, but the market has limited proof against top competition. Put differently, the eye test may see a mature, physical, structurally sound team; the résumé test sees almost no exposure to elite opponents. Both are true. ([warrennolan.com](https://www.warrennolan.com/basketball/2026/team-net-sheet?team=North-Dakota-State))

So the statistical bottom line is this: North Dakota State is a balanced mid-major champion with real functional strengths. They score 80.7 points per game, shoot .468 from the field and .365 from three, own roughly 53-55% eFG depending on source/game pool, rebound well on the offensive glass, and defend at a top-60 national level by efficiency. Their weakness is not one glaring tactical flaw so much as a lack of résumé-confirming data because of a bottom-tier schedule. For tournament forecasting, that makes them more live than their seed line will imply. The numbers say competent offense, dependable defense, and enough rebounding plus perimeter volume to hang around against a more talented favorite. ([gobison.com](https://gobison.com/sports/mens-basketball/stats))
matchup-analyst:
North Dakota State enters the 2026 NCAA Tournament as a perimeter-oriented, ball-sharing offense that still has enough interior size to punish overplays. Their team profile is clear in the season totals: 320 made threes against 876 attempts, so 36.5% of all field-goal attempts are threes, and they average 8.3 assists against 10.8 turnovers per game as a team; on made baskets, they recorded 528 assists on 979 made field goals, an assists-per-FGM rate of 0.539. Individually, the main creators are Andy Stefonowicz (4.9 APG), Damari Wheeler-Thomas (14.4 PPG, 38.5% from three), and Trevian Carson (12.0 PPG, 6.4 RPG, 37.9% from three), while the frontcourt finishers are Markhi Strickland (59.8% FG), Treyson Anderson (50.2% FG, 36.9% from three), and Noah Feddersen (51.2% FG, 5.1 RPG). That construction says NDSU wants to stretch the floor with multiple credible shooters, then let cutters and interior finishers attack the gaps once the help shifts. ([espn.com](https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/team/stats/_/id/2449))

The most reliable way to disrupt that style is to break the passing rhythm, top-lock the wings, and make their guards win with late-clock self-creation instead of advantage passing. The evidence is in their worst offensive games. In the March 7 Summit semifinal loss to Omaha, NDSU scored only 50 points on 15-of-50 shooting and 4-of-26 from three. In the Feb. 28 regular-season loss to North Dakota, they shot 19-of-61 overall and 7-of-34 from three. In the Jan. 17 loss to St. Thomas, they managed just 65 points on 22-of-52 shooting. Those games share the same outcome pattern: when the Bison are driven off clean catch-and-shoot rhythm and forced into more contested perimeter volume, their offense can crater quickly. ([gobison.com](https://gobison.com/sports/mens-basketball/stats))

On press vulnerability: there is not enough primary-source public data in the sources I found to claim a possession-by-possession press-break weakness with confidence. What is supportable is that NDSU is not a high-turnover team overall but can be nudged into sloppier games by aggressive ball pressure. They finished with 366 turnovers in 34 games, or 10.8 per game, while Stefonowicz, their lead passer, also had 67 turnovers, and Wheeler-Thomas and Carson combined for another 100. Against UC Irvine on Dec. 21, NDSU committed 19 turnovers in a 74-73 loss. Against UTEP on Dec. 22, they had 16 turnovers in a 76-66 loss. Against Oral Roberts in the Summit quarterfinal on March 5, they survived 17 turnovers, but The Summit League recap specifically noted they controlled the first half by “taking care of the ball,” then had to re-stabilize after ORU cut the margin to 57-52 in the second half. The actionable takeaway is that pressure matters less because it creates live-ball turnovers every possession and more because it interrupts their timing and shrinks their assist game. ([espn.com](https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/team/stats/_/id/2449))

On zone vulnerability: again, the public game logs do not identify opponent defensive schemes possession by possession, so I cannot honestly label a given loss as definitively “zone-caused.” But the statistical profile suggests how to test them with zone. Because NDSU is heavily perimeter dependent and gets major scoring from shooters such as Wheeler-Thomas, Carson, Stefonowicz, Tay Smith (38.8% from three), and Anderson, a compact zone that stays attached to pick-and-pop spacers can bait them into high-volume three-point nights without rim pressure. Their worst perimeter nights show the danger zone for them: 4-of-26 vs Omaha on March 7, 7-of-34 vs North Dakota on Feb. 28, 6-of-25 at CSU Bakersfield on Dec. 11, 3-of-16 at UTEP on Dec. 22, and 8-of-22 vs South Dakota on Dec. 31 in a 61-point outing. If a zone can keep Feddersen and Strickland from living at the rim while forcing above-the-break threes late in the clock, it can work. ([espn.com](https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/team/stats/_/id/2449))

Preferred pace: NDSU is more comfortable in a controlled, efficient game than in a frantic one. Their team scoring average is 80.7 points, but the better indicator is how their offense performs when the game stays clean and spaced. In wins over Drake (99-94), North Dakota on Feb. 14 (83-66), St. Thomas on Feb. 26 (84-62), and Oral Roberts on March 5 (76-65), they scored efficiently while getting into half-court actions and second-chance offense. Against ORU in the quarterfinal, they scored 38 points in the paint and 23 second-chance points, showing they are not purely jump-shot dependent when the game is played on their terms. To force the opposite, opponents should extend defensive possessions, make NDSU guard multiple actions, and then attack before their half-court defense gets set; when games become more volatile, NDSU has shown slippage, as in the 97-73 loss to Kansas City, the 92-84 loss to Omaha, and the 96-63 loss to North Dakota. ([espn.com](https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/team/stats/_/id/2449))

Size and athleticism mismatches by position are real. At point/lead guard, Stefonowicz is productive but not overpowering physically; bigger, more explosive on-ball defenders can crowd him and force him into a score-first game he does not naturally dominate. At the scoring-guard spots, Wheeler-Thomas and Carson are both sturdy but not especially long, so high-major wings with 6-foot-5 to 6-foot-7 length can bother their pull-up and spot-up windows. In the frontcourt, Anderson is 2.06 m and 111 kg, and Feddersen is 2.08 m and 111 kg, which gives NDSU real size at the 4/5, but it is more strength-and-space size than vertical-rim-protector athleticism. Feddersen averaged only 1.0 blocks per game, Anderson 1.0, and the team just 2.9. That means explosive downhill 4s and 5s can challenge them above the rim, while mobile stretch bigs can pull those two away from the basket. Carson’s 6.4 rebounds per game from the guard line also hints that NDSU needs guards to clean the glass, which can be stressed by superior wing athleticism. ([africa.espn.com](https://africa.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/team/roster/_/id/2449))

Isolation vs team offense: the assist profile strongly suggests team offense over isolation. NDSU’s 528 assists on 979 field goals means 53.9% of made baskets were assisted. Stefonowicz alone has 166 assists, and Carson and Wheeler-Thomas add 181 more combined. That is not an iso-heavy shot diet. Their offense is at its best when the first drive creates the second pass and the second pass creates a catch-and-shoot or interior finish. The counter is to switch selectively off the ball, stay home on second-side shooters, and make Wheeler-Thomas or Carson repeatedly beat defenders one-on-one over size. ([espn.com](https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/team/stats/_/id/2449))

Transition offense and defense: I did not find a trustworthy public 2026 source with exact Synergy-style transition frequency for NDSU, so I will not invent one. What the game evidence does show is that they can score quickly when shotmaking flows, but their best documented postseason win came through paint scoring and offensive rebounding rather than pure transition volume: 38 paint points and 23 second-chance points vs Oral Roberts on March 5. Defensively, their season-long problem is shot quality allowed, especially from three; opponents averaged 71.2 points in the cumulative log segment and regularly posted strong perimeter nights, including Omaha’s 15-of-31 from three on Feb. 7 and North Dakota’s 16-of-29 from three on Feb. 28. That suggests you do not need pure transition to hurt them; early-offense threes and drag-screen actions before the defense is organized are enough. ([thesummitleague.org](https://thesummitleague.org/news/2026/3/6/mens-basketball-top-seeded-ndsu-advances-to-semis-with-win-over-oru.aspx))

Coaching adaptability: Dave Richman’s staff does show evidence of in-game correction. The best example from available sources is the March 5 Summit quarterfinal against Oral Roberts. After ORU used a 10-0 run to cut the margin to 57-52, NDSU responded by holding the Golden Eagles without a field goal for the next seven minutes and re-established control. That is a concrete midgame adjustment result, not a generic coaching platitude. Richman also owns a 19-8 record in the Summit tournament, according to The Summit League, which supports the idea that his staff is organized and tactically steady in repeat-opponent settings. ([thesummitleague.org](https://thesummitleague.org/news/2026/3/6/mens-basketball-top-seeded-ndsu-advances-to-semis-with-win-over-oru.aspx))

Concrete gameplan: To beat this team you must 1) crowd Stefonowicz and deny easy initiations; 2) top-lock Wheeler-Thomas, Carson, and Tay Smith so the first pass does not become a clean catch-and-shoot; 3) tag Feddersen early on duck-ins and box him every shot because NDSU punished ORU with a 16-11 offensive-rebound edge and 23-12 second-chance-point edge; 4) force NDSU into 25-plus three-point attempts, because their offense becomes volatile when the three dominates the shot diet, as shown by 4-of-26 vs Omaha and 7-of-34 vs North Dakota; 5) attack Anderson and Feddersen with movement bigs in pick-and-pop and short-roll coverage, because NDSU blocks only 2.9 shots per game as a team; and 6) push the ball into early offense for trail threes and cross-matches, because NDSU has allowed multiple explosive perimeter games, including Omaha’s 15 made threes and North Dakota’s 16. If an opponent can turn this into a game of late-clock one-on-one offense for the Bison and early-clock spacing decisions for itself, NDSU becomes beatable. ([thesummitleague.org](https://thesummitleague.org/news/2026/3/6/mens-basketball-top-seeded-ndsu-advances-to-semis-with-win-over-oru.aspx))
